The technical challenge that arises when applying Art. 50 II watermarking to synthetic data used for AI training is that watermarks designed to be discernible to humans can impede the integrity of the training data. Specifically, these watermarks may evolve into features that AI systems learn to recognize rather than disregard, jeopardizing the quality of the training process. This creates a conflict between the regulatory requirement for persistent labeling and the need for clean, unadulterated data in model training pipelines.

In comparison, fact-checking systems face their own marking challenges due to the iterative nature of editorial workflows. Watermarks that could satisfy machine-readable requirements are often fragile and likely to be altered or removed during the editing, paraphrasing, and summarization processes common in newsrooms. Unlike the synthetic data case, where a dual-version solution can separate marked and unmarked outputs, fact-checking workflows do not have an equivalent separation point, as human review intervenes between AI generation and publication, destroying the marking required for compliance. 

Thus, both cases highlight significant operational challenges in maintaining compliance with Art. 50 II, but they stem from different sources: synthetic data challenges arise from the conflict between watermarking and training integrity, while fact-checking challenges arise from the fragility of marks in human editorial processes.
